questions.stem: Levothyroxine/liothyronine acts by binding to thyroid receptors. Thyroid hormone receptors belong to which of the following class of receptors?

options.label: A
options.text: Transmembrane receptor linked to tyrosine kinase

questions.solutionHtml:
Thyroid hormone receptors belong to the class of nuclear receptors. 

Nuclear receptors are a family of ligand-regulated transcription factors that are activated by various lipid-soluble signals, including retinoic acid, thyroid hormone, and steroid hormones. They primarily function as transcription factors and directly interact with the genomic DNA to regulate gene expression. 

Nuclear receptors can either remain anchored in the cytoplasm via chaperone proteins until freed by ligand-binding (e.g., steroid and vitamin D receptors) or can reside in the nucleus bound to specific DNA response elements even in the absence of ligand (e.g., thyroid hormone, PPARγ, and retinoic acid receptors).





Goodman & Gillman's The Pharmacological Basis Of Therapeutics - 14th Edition, Page no: 68, 946
Online Resource, https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3578364/

questions.stem: In comparison to thyroxine, liothyronine has ___________.
questions.solutionHtml:
Liothyronine has better absorption compared to levothyroxine. It is almost completely absorbed (100%) when compared to thyroxine (80%).

   Liothyronine(T3)  Levothyroxine(T4)
Onset of action Rapid Slow 
Potency More potent Less potent
Half-life T1/2 -18-24 hr T1/2 - 7-8 days
Source 25% from gland; 75% from peripheral conversion Solely produced by the gland 
Plasma protein binding 0.2% unbound 0.02% unbound

 

Note: Liotrix is a 4:1 mixture of Levothyroxine sodium (LT4): Liothyronine sodium (LT3)

questions.stem: A 23-year-old hypothyroid patient taking levothyroxine regularly has now become pregnant. What would your advice be regarding levothyroxine?

options.label: A
options.text: Switch to liothyronine as levothyroxine is teratogenic

options.label: B
options.text: Increase the dose as pregnancy causes an increased demand for levothyroxine

options.label: C
options.text: Continue the same dose but monitor the serum levels on a fortnightly basis

options.label: D
options.text: Stop levothyroxine till the end of the first trimester as it has teratogenic potential

questions.answerText: Increase the dose as pregnancy causes an increased demand for levothyroxine
questions.solutionHtml:
The dose of levothyroxine in patients who become pregnant should usually be increased. This is because demand for levothyroxine increases in pregnancy and low thyroxine levels are associated with adverse fetal outcomes such as mental retardation. 

The dose of levothyroxine is increased by 30-50% by asking the patient to take 2 extra pills per week. Increased demand for levothyroxine in pregnancy is due to:

  • The increased serum concentration of thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG) induced by estrogen
  • Increased expression of type 3 deiodinase in the placenta
  • A small amount of passage of levothyroxine to the fetus

Thyroid hormones are not teratogenic. Liothyronine is not preferred in pregnancy because T3 has a short half-life and requires frequent dosing to limit large fluctuations in levels. In addition, excess T3 often acts to normalize TSH while lowering T4, thereby risking inadequate T4 availability to the fetus.





Goodman & Gillman's The Pharmacological Basis Of Therapeutics - 13th Edition, Page no: 795

questions.stem: A patient on levothyroxine supplementation would need to increase her dose if she is taking _______.
questions.solutionHtml:
Patients who start estrogen therapy will need to increase their thyroid supplementation doses. 

Estrogens raise the circulating levels of thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG), thereby increasing the bound fraction and decreasing the free (bioactive) fraction of circulating thyroxine (T4). As a consequence, estrogen therapy increases the T4 supplementation requirements of women being treated for primary hypothyroidism.

Drugs increasing TBG levels: 

  • Estrogens
  • Tamoxifen 
  • Methadone
  • 5-fluorouracil  

Drugs decreasing TBG levels: 

  • Androgens
  • Corticosteroids
  • Niacin

Drugs decreasing binding of T4 to TBG (by displacement):

  • Salicylates (aspirin, mefenamic acid) 
  • Heparin
  • Furosemide




Goodman & Gillman's The Pharmacological Basis Of Therapeutics - 13th Edition, Page no: 790

questions.stem: A 45-year-old patient suffering from Graves disease has been on treatment for the past three weeks. She has now developed fever and sore throat with an absolute neutrophil count of 80 neutrophils per microlitre of blood. The use of which of the following drugs can result in such a clinical picture?
questions.solutionHtml:
This patient is suffering from agranulocytosis which is a serious adverse effect that can be seen with the use of either methimazole or propylthiouracil.

Agranulocytosis usually occurs in the initial weeks or months of therapy. It occurs rapidly and periodic monitoring of granulocyte levels is generally ineffective.

However, it is reversible on discontinuation of the drug. Therefore, patients who are on these drugs should be instructed to report immediately if they develop fever or sore throat.

questions.stem: A patient developed thyroid storm in the post-operative ward and was immediately started on IV propranolol and a loading dose of propylthiouracil. The antithyroid drug acts by inhibiting which of the following deiodinases?
questions.solutionHtml:
Propylthiouracil inhibits only type I deiodinase (D1).

Deiodinases are the enzymes that are involved in the peripheral conversion of T4 to either T3 or reverse T3. Type I deiodinase (D1) and type II deiodinase (D2) convert T4 to T3. Type III (D3) is involved in the conversion of T4 to reverse T3. 

Note: Amiodarone inhibits both types I and type II deiodinases. 






Goodman & Gillman's The Pharmacological Basis Of Therapeutics - 13th Edition, Page no. 789

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man presented with complaints of increased sweating and weight loss over the past two months. On examination, he is tachycardic, has exophthalmos, and a diffusely enlarged thyroid gland. Which of the following is the drug of choice for the management of this condition?
questions.solutionHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Graves disease and the drug of choice is methimazole.

Option A: Methimazole is preferred over propylthiouracil due to fewer side effects and single-daily dosing (compared to PTU which is given TID).

Option C: Levothyroxine is used in hypothyroidism.

Option D: Lugol's iodine is a thyroid hormone-release inhibitor but not used as a first-line drug.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old primiparous woman presented with features suggestive of thyrotoxicosis, at 7 weeks of gestation. Which of the following is the drug of choice for the treatment of her condition?
questions.solutionHtml:
The drug of choice for the treatment of thyrotoxicosis during the first trimester of pregnancy is propylthiouracil (PTU). It is because it has lower teratogenic effects than carbimazole or methimazole.

Carbimazole and methimazole are associated with teratogenic effects such as:

  • Aplasia cutis congenita  
  • Choanal atresia
  • Treacheosopageal fistula
  • Fetal goiter

However, propylthiouracil use is limited to the first trimester due to the risk of hepatotoxicity. It is replaced with carbimazole or methimazole in the 2nd and 3rd trimesters of the pregnancy.

The lowest effective antithyroid drug dose should be used throughout gestation. This is to maintain the maternal serum-free T4 level in the upper limit of the non-pregnant normal reference range.

Radioiodine therapy is contraindicated during pregnancy and lactation.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements best describes the Wolff-Chaikoff effect?

options.label: A
options.text: Decrease in thyroid hormone release due to low doses of iodine

options.label: B
options.text: Increase in thyroid hormone release due to high doses of iodine

options.label: C
options.text: Decrease in thyroid hormone synthesis due to high doses of iodine

options.label: D
options.text: Increase in thyroid hormone synthesis due to low iodine intake

questions.answerText: Decrease in thyroid hormone synthesis due to high doses of iodine
questions.solutionHtml:
The Wolff-Chaikoff effect is best described as iodine-induced hypothyroidism.

It is a normal, protective downregulation of thyroid hormone synthesis and release via transient inhibition of iodide organification in the presence of an iodine load (exogenous supplementation, iodinated contrast dye, drugs like amiodarone). This occurs in the thyroid gland which is under pituitary control.

With persistent high iodine load, an escape phenomenon occurs in normal individuals after around 10 days as the iodide levels fall inside the follicle. In autoimmune diseases (Hashimoto’s or Grave’s), however, the suppression may persist.

The Jod-Basedow phenomenon is iodine-induced hyperthyroidism. It is also seen after an iodine load. However, it is seen in thyroid glands where autoregulation and pituitary control have failed. When exposed to an iodine load in excess, instead of blocking the organification process, the thyroid gland (areas of the autonomously functioning gland) continues to uptake the iodine, producing more thyroid hormone independent of normal regulatory mechanisms. It is seen in endemic goiter, toxic multinodular goiter, thyroid adenoma, and sometimes in Grave’s disease.

questions.stem: A patient suffering from Graves disease is posted for thyroidectomy. He is administered iodides preoperatively. What is the primary benefit of administrating iodides in this patient?

options.label: B
options.text: To make the gland firm and less vascular

questions.answerText: To make the gland firm and less vascular
questions.solutionHtml:
The primary benefit of the preoperative use of iodides in Grave’s disease is to make the gland firm and less vascular. This makes manipulation and surgical resection easier.

Antithyroid drugs like methimazole or carbimazole are indicated to render the patient euthyroid.





Goodman & Gillman's The Pharmacological Basis Of Therapeutics - 14th Edition, Page no 952,953
Katzung Basic and Clinical Pharmacology 14th Edition, Page no 695

questions.stem: A patient suffering from hyperthyroidism is administered a drug that acts by inhibiting the release of thyroid hormone. Identify the drug.
questions.solutionHtml:
Potassium iodide inhibits the release of the thyroid hormone.

Iodides of sodium and potassium and Lugol's iodine act by inhibiting thyroid hormone release. Hence, they are also called thyroid constipating agents. They are the fastest-acting agents.

The beneficial effect of iodides peaks over 10-15 days and gradually disappears. Tolerance is hence an issue with the use of iodides.





Goodman & Gillman's The Pharmacological Basis Of Therapeutics - 13th Edition, Page no: 796 , 797 and 798
Katzung Basic and Clinical Pharmacology 14th Edition, Page no : 695

questions.stem: A 43-year-old lady with papillary thyroid cancer is being treated with radioactive iodine 131. What is the half-life of this isotope?
questions.solutionHtml:
The half-life of radioactive I 131 is 8 days

I131 emits both beta and gamma rays. It is used both for diagnostic and therapeutic purposes for thyroid disorders. 

I127 is the stable isotope of iodine. 

I123 is the radioactive isotope of iodine that emits only gamma rays. The action is short-lived with a half-life of around 13 hours. It is indicated for diagnostic indications only. 





Goodman & Gillman's The Pharmacological Basis Of Therapeutics - 13th Edition, Page no: 798

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about Lugol's iodine is incorrect?

options.label: A
options.text: Used to make thyroid gland less vascular

options.label: B
options.text: Used to block thyroid hormone release rapidly

options.label: D
options.text: Augments radioactive iodine uptake into thyroid gland

questions.answerText: Augments radioactive iodine uptake into thyroid gland
questions.solutionHtml:
Lugol's iodine does not augment the uptake of radioactive iodine in the thyroid gland.

Radioactive iodine uptake into the thyroid gland is reduced by Lugol's iodine as the uptake is inversely proportional to the serum concentration of stable iodine.  

Lugol's iodine makes the thyroid gland less vascular and firmer. It blocks the release of thyroid hormone. The beneficial effect peaks over 10-15 days and gradually disappears. Therefore tolerance is an issue.





Goodman & Gillman's The Pharmacological Basis Of Therapeutics - 13th Edition, Page no: 798

questions.stem: A 40-year-old lady who is a known case of Graves disease was posted for thyroidectomy. During the surgery, she developed hyperthermia, agitation and the monitors showed an arrhythmia. She was managed with aggressive IV fluid therapy, ice packs, and multiple drugs. Which of the following drugs that were used, do not inhibit the peripheral conversion of T4 to T3?
questions.solutionHtml:
The given clinical picture is suggestive of a thyrotoxic crisis/thyroid storm. Potassium iodide does not inhibit the peripheral conversion of T4 to T3.

The major action of potassium iodide is the inhibition of hormone release. It is usually given 1 hour after PTU administration to avoid iodine stimulating thyroid hormone synthesis.

Drugs inhibiting the peripheral conversion of T4 to T3 are:

  • Propranolol
  • Glucocorticoids
  • Propylthiouracil
  • Amiodarone
  • Iopanoic acid




Goodman & Gillman's The Pharmacological Basis Of Therapeutics - 14th Edition, Page no: 950
